steps.why: Setting the final velocity to zero is what turns the general equation into a formula for the distance needed to stop.
common_mistakes: Keeping a negative sign inside s = u²/(2a). In that formula a is the magnitude of the retardation; with a signed negative acceleration the relation is s = −u²/(2a), the same positive distance.

recall.must_convey: That stopping distance is the distance travelled after braking until rest, and equals u squared over two a.

steps.memory_tip: Set v = 0 in v² = u² + 2as and the stopping distance falls out.
steps.margin_note: Braking acceleration is negative; in s = u²/(2a) the a is its magnitude.

steps.why: The square on u is why a small rise in speed produces a large rise in stopping distance, which is the reason speed limits matter so much.
common_mistakes: Saying the stopping distance doubles when the speed doubles. It becomes four times larger.

recall.must_convey: That stopping distance goes as the square of the speed and also depends on the braking deceleration.

steps.memory_tip: Twice the speed, FOUR times the stopping distance. The square does it.
steps.margin_note: Give the four-times consequence in words.

insider_note: Use v² = u² + 2as with v = 0. The u² is the point — doubling the speed quadruples the distance.
